prompt:
The escape speed from the surface of the planet Mars is 5.0 x 10^3 m s^-1. In the upper atmosphere of Mars, daytime temperatures reach 260 K. Consider hydrogen gas (H_2, mass of molecule m_H2 = 3.34 x 10^-27 kg) and carbon dioxide gas (CO_2, mass of molecule m_CO2 = 7.30 x 10^-26 kg). Take k = 1.38 x 10^-23 J K^-1.
[FIGURE PLACEHOLDER: Graph of Maxwell-Boltzmann molecular speed distribution showing number of molecules against speed c for a gas at temperature T. The root-mean-square speed c_rms is marked near the peak, and a vertical dashed line marks the escape speed v_esc far out on the high-speed tail.]
(a) Calculate the root-mean-square speed of:
(i) hydrogen molecules at 260 K; [2]
(ii) carbon dioxide molecules at 260 K. [2]
(b) Express each of these root-mean-square speeds as a percentage of the escape speed of Mars. [1]
(c) With reference to the distribution of molecular speeds, explain why hydrogen has escaped from the Martian atmosphere, while carbon dioxide remains the dominant atmospheric gas. [1]

mark_scheme.criterion: (a)(i) Uses c_rms = sqrt(3kT / m) with m = 3.34 x 10^-27 kg and T = 260 K.
(a)(ii) Uses c_rms = sqrt(3kT / m) with m = 7.30 x 10^-26 kg and T = 260 K.
(b) Calculates percentage of escape speed: Hydrogen = (1795 / 5000) * 100% = 35.9% (or 36%); Carbon dioxide = (384 / 5000) * 100% = 7.68% (or 7.7%).

(c) Explains that molecules have a distribution of speeds; for hydrogen, c_rms is a significant fraction (~36%) of escape speed, so a substantial fraction of molecules in the high-speed tail exceed escape speed and escape over geological time; for CO_2, c_rms is only ~7.7% of escape speed, so virtually no molecules reach escape speed.

marking_points.criterion: Substitutes T = 260 K and m = 3.34 x 10^-27 kg into c_rms = sqrt(3kT / m).
Calculates c_rms,H2 = 1800 m s^-1 (or 1795 m s^-1).

part_enrichment.common_pitfall: Omitting the square root or forgetting the factor of 3.

marking_points.criterion: Substitutes T = 260 K and m = 7.30 x 10^-26 kg into c_rms = sqrt(3kT / m).

part_enrichment.common_pitfall: Using molecular mass in grams instead of kilograms.

part_enrichment.guidance: Divide each root-mean-square speed by 5000 m s^-1 and multiply by 100%.
part_enrichment.common_pitfall: Dividing escape speed by c_rms instead of c_rms by escape speed.

marking_points.criterion: Refers to the distribution of speeds and explains that a significant fraction of hydrogen molecules have speeds exceeding escape speed, whereas for CO_2 negligible molecules exceed escape speed.

part_enrichment.guidance: Molecules have a range of speeds (Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution). When c_rms is around 1/3 of escape speed, the high-speed tail continually exceeds escape speed, leading to total atmospheric loss. When c_rms is < 1/10 of escape speed, escape is negligible.
part_enrichment.common_pitfall: Assuming all molecules move at exactly c_rms rather than referring to a distribution of speeds.

hints: In (a), use c_rms = sqrt(3kT / m) for each gas.
In (c), consider the distribution of speeds: do all molecules travel at c_rms, or are some much faster?
solution:
(a)(i) For hydrogen (H_2):
c_rms,H2 = sqrt(3kT / m_H2) = sqrt(3 * (1.38 x 10^-23 J K^-1) * 260 K / (3.34 x 10^-27 kg))
c_rms,H2 = sqrt(1.0764 x 10^-20 / 3.34 x 10^-27) = sqrt(3.2228 x 10^6) = 1795 m s^-1 = 1.80 x 10^3 m s^-1.
(ii) For carbon dioxide (CO_2):
c_rms,CO2 = sqrt(3kT / m_CO2) = sqrt(3 * (1.38 x 10^-23 J K^-1) * 260 K / (7.30 x 10^-26 kg))
c_rms,CO2 = sqrt(1.0764 x 10^-20 / 7.30 x 10^-26) = sqrt(1.4745 x 10^5) = 384 m s^-1.
(b) Percentage of escape speed (5.0 x 10^3 m s^-1):
- Hydrogen: (1795 / 5000) * 100% = 35.9% (or 36%).
- Carbon dioxide: (384 / 5000) * 100% = 7.68% (or 7.7%).
(c) Gas molecules possess a continuous distribution of speeds with a high-speed tail extending well above c_rms. For hydrogen, c_rms is approximately 36% of the escape speed; because this is greater than roughly one-sixth of escape speed, a substantial fraction of molecules in the distribution exceed escape speed and escape into space over geological time. For carbon dioxide, c_rms is only about 7.7% of escape speed; the fraction of CO_2 molecules with speeds exceeding escape speed is negligible, so carbon dioxide is retained.
teacher_walkthrough: Part (a): Compute c_rms for H_2 (1800 m s^-1) and CO_2 (384 m s^-1).
Part (b): Express as percentages: H_2 is ~36% and CO_2 is ~7.7% of escape speed.
Part (c): Apply Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution concepts: when c_rms > v_esc / 6, significant escape occurs over time; CO_2 is far below this threshold and is retained.
